en: Regarding the Dharma for Brahmā’s Selection of the Site:
I have carefully examined the *Mahābrahmādeva-rahasya-sūtra*, which states that when the Tathāgata was on the bodhisattva path,
during five million lifetimes as a mantra-holding rishi, he frequently traveled among various mountains to dwell in seclusion in pure locations.

In his chamber, he was constantly visited by Brahmā deities who came to attend upon him, and there were also devas, nāgas, and the eight classes of beings who appeared before him. Nevertheless, despite these auspicious signs, he was still afflicted by Māra; his dharma practices were not accomplished. Sometimes, when reciting mantras, they were distorted due to a lack of purity;
sometimes he practiced the Mūdrā rites; and sometimes he could not find a suitable site for the maṇḍala. For these reasons, his practices frequently failed to succeed.

Now, examining the sūtras, there are forty-two methods for selecting a site that are capable of forming a maṇḍala, enabling the mantra-holders to accomplish their dharmas as they wish; those who do not obtain these methods will merely waste their days and months in vain.
First: deep within a mountain cave, there is rock on all four sides with earth at its center, appearing as if someone had swept the ground; this is the place where the Sage attained enlightenment.

From the center of the ground, extraordinary flowers emerge; this ground is the foremost. By establishing an altar here and reciting mantras with meditative concentration, one will certainly move the Tathāgatas.
A bhikṣu who maintains the precepts may obtain the dharmas of this ground; one who does not maintain the precepts shall not obtain them on this ground—be careful of this.
Second: In deep mountains where there are large beasts, lions, and fierce predators, and where no grass grows upon the ground, that place must be the dwelling of a sage.
The various beasts were all deities who protect the stupa; having established an altar at this site, the ritual was successfully completed.

In the fifth year of the Kaihuang era, I entered Guangzhou and found this place in the deep mountains. Following the previous rites for its consecration, there appeared a person with a golden body wearing white robes; the great deity stood over three *zhang* tall. Startled and terrified, I was told by the person: "I am the deity of the Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa.
Seeing that you now sit upon this blessed ground, I have manifested my form out of sympathetic resonance, coming here to receive your dharma."

Third: Ascending to the high summit of the mountain, one sees a large rock as smooth and polished as a grinding stone, upon which the reflection of a human figure appears; this rock is the auspicious stone of the Sage.

Take white *māo* grass to make a mat; sit in the northwest corner and recite the mantra while performing the ritual, and success will be achieved. No monk who does not maintain the precepts is permitted to sit there.

Fourth: if the four sides of the mountain are covered with grass, wood, and forests, but the center is devoid of objects and as clean as a person has swept the ground, the altar established there will certainly achieve success.
Fifth: Within the mountain, five-colored stones were seen—blue, yellow, red, white, and black—each situated in its respective direction; this was the place where a sage practiced the Way.
This ground must be superior, for when an altar was constructed, the Four Heavenly Kings arrived in person.

Sixth: Enter the mountains and find a place where a snake with horns on its head coils upon a rock; where the snake lies there is no grass, and it rises and departs as soon as it sees a person coming—this is the most excellent site for constructing an altar.

Seventh: In the mountains, one sees a white deer lying on the ground; for a space of about one zhang in every direction there is no grass or wood, and this spot is also suitable for constructing an altar.
Eighth: If one sees in the mountains a place where a white deer lies down, with no grass or trees on all four sides, such a sign indicates it is a site for constructing an altar. Ninth:

In the mountains there was a person over one zhang tall, wearing black robes and having four eyes on his face, sitting upon a rock; the surface of that rock was so clear and bright that it reflected the image of the person's face, and whenever a bhikṣu ascended, he would surely succeed.

Tenth: Within the mountain there was an old man with white hair; his eyebrows and beard were entirely white, and he watched the place where [the practitioner] was walking. Wherever his gaze fell, no grasses or trees grew; this ground is fit to serve as a ritual altar (*maṇḍala*), whereas ground with grasses and trees is unfit.

Eleventh: If one sees stones within a mountain, or five-colored clouds emerging from within the earth—not during times of rain or overcast weather—this location is certainly where a sage sat; it is excellent for constructing an altar.
Twelfth: Within the mountains there is a stone chamber where lions and fierce beasts dwell, and where no grass or trees grow; this site is fit to serve as a ritual altar.
Thirteenth: Within the mountain there is a level place devoid of grass; if the ground bears human footprints measuring one chi or more, it is fit to serve as a ritual altar. Fourteenth:
Entering a mountain valley, he saw grass growing upon the ground that appeared as if someone were sitting upon it; when the tips of the grass bent downward, it was deemed suitable. Fifteenth:
Entering a mountain peak or a level plain, he saw extraordinary flowers emerging from all four directions, with a vacant space about eight feet across at the center; that place was wondrous.

Sixteenth: In the mountains, there are places where flowers emerge; these are the seats where sages sit. Without distinction between spring, summer, autumn, or winter, extraordinary flowers appear at all times. Whenever such flowers bloom, they differ from common blossoms, and the ground itself is wondrous.
Seventeenth: While reciting mantras in the mountains, he saw a white light emerge from the ground; there was no grass on all four sides, and he thought, "This place is wonderful. Eighteenth:
In the mountains, one perceives fragrances at inappropriate times, and the ground appears as if smoke is rising;
this place is wondrous. Nineteenth:
within the mountains, there are five-colored lights that emerge from the earth or from the rocks; observing their locations, the sites of emergence are wondrous.

Twenty: If one sees peacocks or various other birds in the mountains carrying grass and assorted flowers in their beaks to offer them at a site, that ground is fit and is a place where a noble person has emerged; it is excellent.
Twenty-first: In a mountain where there are places of five-colored soil, go there at dawn on the following day; if five-colored light emerges, this place is suitable. Twenty-second:
In the mountains, one sees four white cranes; where they sit facing one another, there is no grass—this is the site for establishing the altar.
Twenty-third: In the mountains, one sees two trees standing opposite each other, with a form resembling a human figure between them; that ground is suitable.
Twenty-fourth: One sees a yellow ox or a white ox lying on the ground in the mountains; the ground is devoid of growing grass, appearing as if swept by someone, and the ground is level.
Twenty-fifth: In the mountains there is a stone that produces the sound of a bell when struck;
that place is suitable. Twenty-sixth:
If one sees a cave in the mountains, it is excellent if there is no echo when one calls out from within;
if there is an echo, it is not so. Twenty-seventh:
If there is a temple or observatory among the mountains and its ground is level and clear, it is suitable to observe five-colored lights before the sun has risen.
Twenty-eighth: In the mountains, he saw a divine person wearing celestial robes at the place where [the water] emerged;
it was sufficient. Twenty-ninth:
If there is earth within a mountain, heaped up like an anthill to a height of five chi or less, it is suitable. The thirtieth:
if one sees stones or earth within a mountain shaped like a dragon, or if there is on the ground what appears to be a painted design, it is suitable.
Thirty-first: Seeing in the mountains a rishi, or a person or beast with horns; observing the ground from which they emerge, it is suitable. Thirty-second:

At an improper time and in an improper place, if one sees light suddenly emerge, or if there is someone who has violated the precepts against fire, or if there is the scent of incense smoke, this is a site where an Arhat attained the Way; it is worthy [of veneration].

Thirty-third: If one enters a monastery or establishes an altar in a layperson’s home, the merit is not even a hundredth or a thousandth of that obtained in the mountains; yet, if one wishes to save sentient beings, one must ultimately choose the proper location.

At the Gaolam Monastery atop the mountain, one must dig two feet deep into the ground; if bones are found within, it is deemed unfit for use, but if tiles or stones are found, one may then bury the seven treasures within the earth before finally utilizing the site.
Thirty-fourth: If one digs into the earth to a depth of three feet and finds a small amount of unusual objects or treasures, it is called "superior ground" and is fit for use. Thirty-fifth:

Dig the ground to a depth of two feet; where there is nothing within the earth, construct an altar. Take the soil removed from within that ground, sift it thoroughly, mix it with powdered incense, and firmly compact it.
Thirty-sixth: This ground is suitable because it has never been inhabited or used as a place for sleeping or lying down. Thirty-seventh:
Within the ground, one must never establish caves, pits, stoves, or places where chickens and dogs lie;
this is permissible. Thirty-eighth:
At the fifth watch, observe the atmospheric conditions within the ground; if there is black light, it is not permissible.
Regarding those who emit light from outside [the body], they are capable. Number Thirty-nine:

If one constructs a ritual altar (*maṇḍala*) in a layperson’s home, it often fails to accord with the Dharma and results in injury; neither the mantra-master nor the other party will derive any benefit. One must simply perform the boundary-binding (*sīmā-bandha*) and need not construct an altar; I have personally verified that such cases have indeed resulted in loss.

Fortieth: If it is necessary to construct a mandala, one must cause the patient to become pure; they should bathe daily and wear fresh, clean garments, sitting alone in a separate room. The mantra-master, following the previous procedure, selects a site to construct the mandala and recites the dharma with single-minded focus while calling out the name [of the deity]; the patient must not be allowed to see within the mandala.
If one brings the patient into the altar area, it will also harm the mantra-practitioner.
Forty-one: If a bhikṣu who maintains the precepts recites mantras and constructs an altar, he is a hundred thousand times superior to a layperson.
If, after selecting a site and constructing a single altar, that ground remains undestroyed even when the calamities of the kalpa arise, it is so. Forty-second:

If one constructs a water altar, there is no need to perform the ritual of selection; however, one must choose an exceptionally superior location, for if such a site cannot be obtained, there will ultimately be no benefit or success.
The *Brahmadeva-dharaṇī-bhūmi-vidhi* is completed. The *Ryūun-un* (Clouds of Spiritual Clouds) collation notes state:
"On the twentieth day of the second month in the fourth year of the Jōkyō era, the first proofreading was finished by Shōgon at age forty-nine."
